title: The Lesson I Learned From the Burning Bush
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From the Burning Bush
The Day God Spoke Through Fire, and the Truth That Changed Everything About My Scandal, My Calling, and My Grace
There are moments in Scripture that feel less like ancient history and more like a mirror.
The burning bush is one of those moments.
Most people remember the miracle.
The fire.
The voice.
The holy ground.
But the longer I walk with Christ, the more I realize the story was never primarily about a bush that burned without being consumed.
It was about a broken man who thought his life was over.
Maybe that is why this story hits differently when you've failed.
When you've disappointed people.
When you've ruined opportunities.
When you've carried regret long enough for it to become part of your identity.
Because before Moses ever stood before Pharaoh, before the Red Sea parted, before miracles shook nations, Moses was living in exile.
Hidden.
Forgotten.
Disqualified in his own mind.
And that's where many of us secretly live.
Not physically.
Spiritually.
We smile in public while privately believing God can use everyone except us.
We sing worship songs while silently replaying old mistakes.
We tell others about grace while struggling to receive it ourselves.
That is why the burning bush matters.
Not because of the fire.
Because of what God does with failures.
The story begins in Exodus 3.
Moses had spent approximately forty years tending sheep in Midian after fleeing Egypt.
The prince had become a shepherd.
The man who once lived in a palace now wandered deserts.
The deliverer was hiding from his destiny.
Then everything changed.
Scripture says:
"Now Moses was tending the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian..." (Exodus 3:1)
Nothing extraordinary.
Nothing dramatic.
Just another ordinary day.
And that may be the first lesson from the burning bush.
God often shows up when life feels painfully ordinary.
We expect Him in stadiums.
He often meets us in deserts.
We expect Him in crowds.
He often speaks in isolation.
We expect Him after we have everything together.
He often comes while we are still trying to figure out who we are.
Then Moses sees something impossible.
"The angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush." (Exodus 3:2)
The Hebrew word for bush is seneh (סְנֶה).
A common desert shrub.
Nothing impressive.
Nothing majestic.
Nothing that would attract attention.
And perhaps that is intentional.
Because God has always loved using ordinary things to reveal extraordinary glory.
A manger.
A fishing boat.
A cross.
A tomb.
A shepherd's staff.
A burning bush.
And people like us.
The bush burned.
Yet it was not consumed.
Fire throughout Scripture often represents God's holy presence.
Yet what captivates Moses is not merely the fire.
It is the fact that the bush remains standing.
The presence of God is intense enough to burn yet merciful enough to preserve.
That truth alone could heal countless hearts.
Some people are convinced that if God truly came near, they would be destroyed by shame.
Exposed by guilt.
Condemned by failure.
But the burning bush reveals something beautiful.
God's holiness does not exist merely to consume sinners.
It exists to transform them.
The fire burns.
The bush remains.
And suddenly I see my own story.
I should have been consumed by pride.
Consumed by rebellion.
Consumed by mistakes.
Consumed by sin.
Yet somehow, through Christ, grace preserved me.
The fire came.
But mercy remained.
Then God speaks.
"Moses, Moses."
In Hebrew, repetition carries intimacy and urgency.
Just as later Scripture says:
"Abraham, Abraham."
"Samuel, Samuel."
"Martha, Martha."
"Simon, Simon."
The God of the universe calls him by name.
Not his failure.
Not his shame.
Not his worst moment.
His name.
Because God knows who you are even when you have forgotten.
Then comes one of the most profound statements in Scripture.
"Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground." (Exodus 3:5)
The Hebrew word for holy is qadosh (קָדוֹשׁ).
Set apart.
Sacred.
Different.
The ground was not holy because of dirt.
It was holy because God was there.
And this changes everything.
Many people spend their lives searching for holy places.
But holiness is ultimately about God's presence.
A prison cell can become holy.
A hospital room can become holy.
A living room can become holy.
A broken heart can become holy.
Anywhere God meets a person becomes sacred ground.
Then God reveals His identity.
In Exodus 3:14, He says:
"Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh" (אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה).
Often translated:
"I AM WHO I AM."
More literally, the phrase carries the sense of:
"I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE."
The self-existent One.
The eternal One.
The One who depends on nothing.
The One before whom every kingdom rises and falls.
The One whose existence is not borrowed.
The One who simply is.
Centuries later Jesus would intentionally echo this truth.
Before Abraham was, "ἐγώ εἰμι" (ego eimi)—"I AM." (John 8:58)
The crowd immediately understood the claim.
Jesus was not merely identifying Himself.
He was identifying Himself with the God of the burning bush.
The same God who called Moses.
The same God who delivered Israel.
The same God who entered human history to rescue sinners.
The same God who hung on a cross for us.
And that is where the burning bush ultimately points.
To Jesus.
Because Moses' greatest problem was not Pharaoh.
It was inadequacy.
Again and again Moses protests.
"I am not qualified."
"I am not enough."
"I cannot speak."
"I cannot do this."
Sound familiar?
Most believers do not struggle because God is weak.
They struggle because they think their weakness disqualifies them.
But God's answer was never, "Moses, you're stronger than you think."
God's answer was:
"I will be with you."
That changes everything.
The power was never Moses.
The power was God's presence.
And the same remains true today.
The Kingdom of God has never advanced because people were impressive.
It advances because Christ is.
The Gospel is not a story about capable people doing great things for God.
It is the story of a great God rescuing incapable people.
This is why the burning bush still burns in the hearts of believers thousands of years later.
Because it whispers something many of us desperately need to hear.
Your scandal is not stronger than His grace.
Your past is not stronger than His purpose.
Your failure is not stronger than His mercy.
Your wounds are not stronger than His redemption.
Moses had blood on his hands.
David had moral failure in his history.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted believers.
Yet God rewrote their stories.
Not because sin did not matter.
It did.
Not because justice did not matter.
It did.
But because grace was greater.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Romans 5:20 says:
"Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more."
The Greek word is hyperperisseuō (ὑπερπερισσεύω).
Grace did not merely match sin.
Grace overflowed beyond it.
Grace exceeded it.
Grace overwhelmed it.
That is why our mission remains simple.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe today you feel like Moses in Midian.
Forgotten.
Disappointed.
Spiritually exhausted.
Convinced your best days are behind you.
If so, hear the voice from the bush.
God is still calling names.
God is still restoring failures.
God is still transforming deserts into holy ground.
God is still writing redemption stories.
And perhaps your story is not ending.
Perhaps it is finally beginning.
If this message spoke to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
What part of your life are you trusting Jesus to rewrite?
You may be surprised how many people are fighting the same battle.
Not because the Gospel can be purchased—it cannot.
Salvation is the free gift of God through Jesus Christ alone.
One encounter with God's presence can turn a wilderness into a calling.
